Adit Pay Dispute Handling SOP (Adit Pay)

ADIT PAY

Dispute Handling SOP

A guide for T2 Support agents handling card disputes on Adit Pay, for active and off-boarded practices.

Field Detail
Version 1.0 (Draft)
Owner Adit Pay Team (Manager: Sebastin)
Applies to All Adit Pay support agents (Calls Wing & Chat Wing)
Status Interim guidance: Part 3 (off-boarded clients) reflects current system behaviour, pending a product decision on the notification gap (see Section 6)

1. Purpose & Scope

This SOP explains how card disputes work on Adit Pay, what an agent needs to do when one lands on a ticket, and how the process differs for a practice that has already been off-boarded. It exists because the off-boarded case currently has no automated notification path. Agents are the only safety net until a permanent fix ships.

Use this document when:

  • A dispute-related ticket comes in from a practice, a patient, or is flagged internally in Asana/Slack.

  • You need to explain a Stripe payout, withdrawal, or negative balance debit to a client.

  • You are deciding whether a case needs escalation to the Adit Pay specialist on duty (e.g. Sandy Clark) or to the Adit Pay manager.

2. Key Terms, In Plain Language

Term What it means
Dispute / Chargeback The cardholder’s bank pulls money back from the merchant on the cardholder’s behalf while it investigates a complaint (e.g. “service not received”).
Dispute fee A flat $15 fee Stripe charges the connected account every time a dispute is opened, win or lose.
Transfer reversal Stripe clawing back the original payout amount from the practice’s Stripe balance when a dispute is lost.
Negative balance What’s left in the connected account after a reversal + fee are deducted, if the account doesn’t have enough funds sitting in it already.
Debit negative balances: On An account setting that lets Stripe auto-pull a negative balance straight from the practice’s own linked bank account rather than leaving it unpaid.
Withdrawn (payout status) The label Stripe shows when it has pulled funds from the practice’s bank account to cover a negative balance. It is not a new charge, it is Stripe recovering money already reversed.
Evidence deadline The date by which the merchant must submit proof to contest the dispute. Set per-case by the card network, usually 7-21 days after the dispute opens.

3. How a Dispute Works: Active Client

This is the default, fully automated flow for any practice that is still live on Adit Pay.

3.1 When a dispute is opened

  1. A patient contacts their bank and disputes a charge.

  2. Stripe notifies Adit. The disputed amount is reversed out of the practice’s Stripe balance, and a $15 dispute fee is charged.

  3. The payment is marked Disputed in Adit Pay and appears on the practice’s Disputes screen.

  4. If the payment was a payment plan instalment, that instalment is marked disputed too.

  5. Notifications go out (see the table below).

3.2 Who gets notified

Event Patient email Practice email In-app
Dispute created Yes: “Payment Dispute” Yes: “Important: Dispute Notification, Response Required by {date}” + help link Yes: “Payment Dispute: {location}”
Dispute won Not sent Yes: “Adit Pay, Dispute Won” Not sent
Dispute lost Not sent Yes: “Adit Pay, Dispute Lost” Not sent

Note: the practice email only sends if that location has payment notifications turned on and has at least one notification address saved in its Adit Pay preferences.

3.3 What the practice can do

From the Disputes section in Adit Pay, the practice can:

  • View disputes grouped as Needs Response / In Review / All / Won / Lost.

  • Submit evidence to fight the dispute, with the response deadline shown.

  • Accept the dispute (closes it as a loss).

  • Email the patient directly.

3.4 Outcomes

Known product gap (applies to all clients, not just off-boarded)

When a dispute is won, Adit returns the disputed amount to the practice but does not currently return the $15 dispute fee, even though Stripe returns that fee to Adit. This is a separate open item, flag it if a client asks why the fee wasn’t refunded on a win.

Outcome What happens to the payment What happens to the money
Won Status returns to Paid Disputed amount is returned to the practice
Lost Stays Disputed Nothing, the money was already pulled back at the start
Warning closed Treated the same as Won Amount returned to the practice

4. How a Dispute Works: Off-Boarded Client

This is the part that needs manual agent attention There is currently no automated notification for a dispute on an off-boarded account, to the patient, the practice, or anyone at Adit. The money still moves exactly as it would for an active client. You are the control here until a product fix ships.

4.1 What still happens automatically

  • The disputed amount is still pulled back from the practice’s connected account, every time.

  • The $15 dispute fee is still charged, every time.

  • If the connected account balance can’t cover it and “Debit negative balances” is On, Stripe pulls the shortfall from the practice’s own linked bank account (this shows as a Withdrawn payout).

  • If “Debit negative balances” is Off, or the practice’s bank details are no longer valid, the shortfall becomes Adit’s platform liability instead.

4.2 What does NOT happen automatically

  • No dispute email to the patient.

  • No dispute email to the practice.

  • No alert to anyone at Adit, nothing today triggers this into a queue.

The reason changes over time but the result is the same: while the practice’s data is still in the system, the notification is deliberately suppressed by an intentional rule. Once the data has been deleted as part of off-boarding, the notification step fails outright and the error only goes to a log file, it is never surfaced to a person. From Stripe’s side, the whole thing looks successful. There is no retry and no alarm.

4.3 The asymmetry to watch for: money returned on a win

Money pulled back always happens, active or off-boarded. Money returned on a win does not behave the same way. Returning funds relies on Adit’s own record that the money was taken from that practice in the first place. If that record has been deleted along with the rest of the off-boarded client’s data, the return step is silently skipped, Stripe credits the amount back to Adit’s platform balance, and it simply stays there. The practice can end up out of pocket for the full disputed amount plus the $15 fee on a dispute that was actually won, and nothing anywhere flags it. If you are handling a won dispute for an off-boarded practice, manually verify the refund actually reached the practice’s account, do not assume it did.

Late wins add a second version of this risk Per Stripe’s own documentation, a dispute’s status can occasionally flip from lost back to won after the fact (a “late win”), when the issuer credits or debits Stripe outside the normal lifecycle. Stripe cannot predict when this happens. For an off-boarded client with no one monitoring the account, a late win can land funds back with Adit and go completely unnoticed, the same silent-skip risk as 4.3, just triggered later and with no dispute ticket open to prompt anyone to check.

4.4 Stripe’s dispute timeline (for setting expectations)

Stage Typical window
Payment → patient can still raise a dispute Usually up to 120 days from the transaction (see note below)
Dispute raised → evidence deadline 7-21 days, varies by card network; Stripe sets an exact date per case
Evidence submitted → issuer’s decision A further 60-75 days
Full lifecycle, start to finish 2-3 months. Stripe does not support arbitration, so a lost dispute cannot be appealed further

The 120-day window is not a hard ceiling. For anything paid in advance of the service, the clock starts on the service date, not the payment date, which matters for treatment plan deposits and booking deposits. Some non-card payment methods allow up to 180 days. A dispute raised on day 120 can still be active roughly seven months after the original payment, later still for prepaid future appointments.

5. Step-by-Step: Handling a Dispute Ticket

5.1 Active client

  1. Confirm the dispute in the Adit Pay Disputes screen for that location and note the response deadline.

  2. Loop in the practice if they haven’t already engaged, point them to the Disputes screen so they can submit their own evidence.

  3. If the practice wants Adit’s help interpreting the dispute reason, explain the reason code in plain terms and what kind of evidence typically helps (proof of delivery/service for “not received” claims).

  4. Track the response deadline. If it’s close and the practice hasn’t acted, escalate to the Adit Pay specialist handling the case.

  5. Once Stripe returns a decision, confirm the payment status updated correctly in Adit Pay and that any owed refund actually reached the practice.

5.2 Off-boarded client: interim manual process

Until the notification gap in Section 4.2 is fixed, treat every off-boarded dispute as something that will not surface on its own. It typically reaches an agent one of two ways: an internal flag in Slack/Asana (as with the Seville Dental case), or the former client contacting Support directly after noticing an unexplained withdrawal.

  1. Pull the dispute directly from the Stripe Dashboard (connected account → Payments → the disputed payment) since it won’t appear in Adit Pay’s Disputes screen the normal way.

  2. Check the connected account balance and “Debit negative balances” setting to determine whether the practice’s own bank will absorb the reversal, or whether it falls to Adit’s platform account. Flag to your lead immediately if it’s the latter.

  3. Since the former client has no Adit Pay login, they cannot submit evidence themselves. If they want to contest the dispute, gather evidence from them by email (proof of service delivery, appointment records, prior communication with the patient) and submit it on their behalf through the Stripe Dashboard before the deadline.

  4. If the deadline has already passed with no evidence submitted, the dispute is lost by default and cannot be reopened or appealed, Stripe’s decision at that point is final. The only remaining avenue is the cardholder voluntarily asking their own bank to withdraw the dispute; that request has to come from the patient, not from Adit or the practice.

  5. If the dispute is won, manually verify that the refunded amount actually reaches the practice’s linked bank account. Do not assume the automated return step ran, see Section 4.3.

  6. Log the case in the shared Asana tracker so Product has visibility into volume while the permanent fix is being scoped.

6. Escalation Matrix

Pending product decision

Product has been asked (Arbazkhan Pathan, per “Disputes for Off-Boarded Clients”) to decide the long-term fix, options under discussion include retaining minimal dispute-relevant data through the full window, routing off-boarded disputes to a queue for Support, and confirming what happens to a practice’s Stripe connected account at

Situation Escalate to
Dispute on an active client, response deadline is close and practice is unresponsive Adit Pay specialist on duty (e.g. Sandy Clark)
Dispute on an off-boarded client, any case Adit Pay specialist on duty for manual handling (per Section 5.2)
Connected account balance insufficient and “Debit negative balances” is Off, potential platform liability Adit Pay manager (Sebastin) + Vatsal Shah / Ali Jhaver
Won dispute, off-boarded client, refund did not visibly reach the practice Adit Pay manager (Sebastin) + Engineering (data retention / notification gap)
Client disputes the accuracy of a support explanation already given (e.g. a prior call/email) Pull the original ticket/call notes before replying, confirm what was actually said before sending anything new in writing

7. Client Communication Templates

7.1 Explaining a dispute to an active or off-boarded client

Use plain language. Avoid “the dispute was processed” without saying what that means in dollars.

“A dispute was opened by the patient’s bank on {date}. As part of that process, the original payment amount of {amount} plus a $15 dispute fee were reversed from your account. Because the case was not contested before the {deadline} deadline, the decision is now final and cannot be reopened. If you have documentation showing the service was delivered, the remaining option is for the patient to contact their bank directly and request the dispute be withdrawn.”

7.2 Explaining a “Withdrawn” payout line

“This withdrawal is not a new charge. It reflects our processor recovering a negative balance created when a dispute was lost, the original payment plus the $15 dispute fee. Because your account is set to cover negative balances automatically, this was drawn from your linked bank account rather than left outstanding.”

7.3 What not to say

  • Don’t confirm a notification email was sent to the practice unless you have verified it in the system for that specific case, off-boarded accounts typically do not receive one (Section 4.2).

  • Don’t imply the dispute can be reopened or appealed by Adit once the deadline has passed, it cannot (Section 4.4).

  • Don’t promise a refund timeline on a won dispute for an off-boarded client without manually checking it landed, see Section 4.3.

8. Client Dispute Notification Emails (3-Touchpoint Sequence)

Active clients get these three notifications automatically (Section 3.2). Off-boarded clients get none of them automatically (Section 4.2), so for any off-boarded case, an agent must send all three manually, at the same points in the timeline an active client would have received them. Do not skip a step, each one creates a record that the client was given a fair chance to respond.

8.1 Touchpoint 1: Dispute Opened (send as soon as the dispute is found)

Subject: Action Required: Payment Dispute Opened for {Practice Name} (Response Needed by {evidence_deadline})

Hi {Contact Name},A payment dispute has been opened against a transaction processed through Adit Pay while your account was active with us. Because your account is no longer active, this did not reach you automatically, we are sending it manually so you have a fair opportunity to respond.Dispute details:Patient: {Patient Name}Amount disputed: {amount} (plus a $15 dispute fee)Reason: {dispute_reason}Dispute opened: {open_date}Evidence deadline: {evidence_deadline}If you have documentation showing the service or product was delivered (appointment records, treatment notes, prior communication with the patient), please send it to us before the deadline above and we will submit it on your behalf. If we do not hear from you by the deadline, the dispute will be resolved automatically in the cardholder’s favor and cannot be reopened afterward.Best regards,{Agent Name}Adit Pay Support

8.2 Touchpoint 2: Evidence Deadline Reminder (send 2-3 days before the deadline if no response yet)

Subject: Reminder: {days_remaining} Days Left to Respond to Dispute for {Practice Name}

Hi {Contact Name},This is a follow-up to our earlier email about the payment dispute for {Patient Name} ({amount}). We have not yet received a response.The evidence deadline is {evidence_deadline}, {days_remaining} days from today. After this date, the decision becomes final and cannot be appealed or reopened, regardless of the circumstances.If you have supporting documentation, please send it to us as soon as possible so we can submit it before the deadline. If you do not intend to contest this dispute, no action is needed and it will resolve automatically.Best regards,{Agent Name}Adit Pay Support

8.3 Touchpoint 3: Outcome Notification (send as soon as Stripe returns a decision)

Subject: Dispute {Won / Lost}: {Practice Name}, {Patient Name}

Hi {Contact Name},The dispute for {Patient Name} ({amount}) has been resolved.Outcome: {Won / Lost}If won: the disputed amount of {amount} has been returned to your account. Please allow a few business days for it to reflect. Note that the $15 dispute fee is not refunded, this is standard across all Adit Pay accounts.If lost: the disputed amount and $15 fee remain deducted, consistent with the dispute reversal that occurred when the case opened. This decision is final and cannot be appealed through Adit or Stripe. The only remaining option is for the patient to contact their card issuer directly and request a withdrawal of the dispute.Please let us know if you have any questions about this outcome.Best regards,{Agent Name}Adit Pay Support

Off-boarded cases: verify touchpoint 3 before closing the ticket For an off-boarded client, sending the outcome email is not enough on its own. Before closing the ticket, confirm in Stripe that a won dispute’s funds actually reached the practice’s account (Section 4.3). Do not rely on the automated return step, it does not run reliably for off-boarded accounts.

Source for Part 1-2 content: internal document “Disputes for Off-Boarded Clients: Current Behaviour.” Stripe timeline reference: docs.stripe.com/disputes/how-disputes-work. This SOP will be updated once Product finalizes the off-boarded dispute handling decision.

Adit-Pay-ACH-and-CF-Training-QA-Manual (Adit Pay)

ACH & Convenience Fees: Training, Coaching & QA Manual

Part 1: Training & Coaching Guide

1. Payments

Why it matters: this is the list every agent lives in day to day. If the fee columns are wrong or missing, agents can’t answer a practice’s most common question. “why did this patient pay more than the invoice?”. Without digging into the detail page.

Walkthrough

  1. Open Adit Pay -> Payments. It defaults to the “All” tab.

  2. Glance at the KPI row up top: Amount Processed, Convenience Fees, Processing Fees, Refunds, Disputed.

  3. Each row should show Service Amount and Conv. Fee as two separate columns, not one combined “Amount.”

  4. Every row needs a Method column too, showing Card or Bank.

  5. Select a group and click “Select All”. The header should read “ALL Requests Selected,” not a row count.

Payments list: new fee columns, plus the card-present / card-not-present fee formulas

Fee math you’ll be asked about

  • Card-not-present (2.9% + $0.30): Final Charge = (Desired Amount + $0.30) / (1 - 0.029). A $100 service becomes $103.30. Adit’s processor takes $3.30, the practice nets exactly $100.

  • Card-present (2.25% + $0.20): Final Charge = (Desired Amount + $0.20) / (1 - 0.0225). A $100 service becomes $102.51.

Talk track

Q: Why is this patient’s Convenience Fee different from another patient who paid the same amount?

A: Card-present and card-not-present transactions use different formulas (2.25%+$0.20 vs. 2.9%+$0.30). Two patients paying the same service amount through different channels will see different fees. That’s expected.

Q: Can I see fees broken out by location?

A: Yes. The KPI tiles and the Conv. Fee column are both scoped to whatever location filter is active at the top of the page.

Watch for: a Bank-method payment showing a non-zero Convenience Fee anywhere in the live product.

This should never happen. Flag it to engineering immediately (see QA-2). Convenience Fees never apply to Bank/ACH.

Common pitfalls

  • Don’t confuse “Service Amount” with “Paid Amount” when reading a row aloud to a practice. Paid Amount includes the fee, Service Amount doesn’t.

  • If a practice asks for a report, confirm whether they want Service Amount totals or Paid Amount totals before exporting. They’re not interchangeable for accounting purposes.

2. Payments Details Page

Why it matters: this is where a practice goes to resolve a billing dispute with a patient. Every number here needs to be traceable and consistent with the receipt the patient already has in hand.

Walkthrough

  1. From the Payments list, click any row to open its Details page.

  2. Remember the list-format rule: every tab except “Paid” displays the requested date; the “Paid” tab shows the paid date instead.

  3. Read the transaction table columns left to right: Type -> Payment Method -> Service Amount -> Conv Fee -> Total Amount -> Processing Fees -> Net.

  4. The Payment Details panel below should follow the same order: Service Amount -> Convenience Fee -> Total Amount -> Processing Fee -> Net -> Status.

  5. For a refund, use Actions -> Initiate Refund. The refund amount defaults to Total Amount (including any fee). Check with the practice before changing it.

Payment Details Page: format spec and Convenience Fee breakdown

Talk track

Q: The patient says they were charged more than their invoice. What happened?

A: Walk them to the Payment Details panel and read Service Amount, then Convenience Fee, then Total Amount in that order. The invoice amount is the Service Amount, and the difference is the disclosed Convenience Fee.

Q: Can we refund just the fee and not the service amount?

A: The practice can choose to refund the entire amount including the fee, but only the amount up to the original service amount should ever post back to the ledger. Confirm this with the practice before processing a partial refund.

Common pitfalls

  • Don’t read the Requested Date on the Paid tab. It shows Paid Date instead, and quoting the wrong date to a practice erodes trust fast.

3. Payment Receipt

Why it matters: the receipt is the patient’s proof of what they agreed to pay. If the fee isn’t itemized here, support fields far more “why was I overcharged” tickets than necessary.

Walkthrough

  1. Open any Paid transaction and click Receipt (top right of the detail page).

  2. The receipt should show, in order: Transaction ID, Paid On, Patient Name, Payment Method, Service Amount, Convenience Fee, Total Amount Paid.

  3. The internal practice notification should mirror the same breakdown, so front-desk staff see identical numbers to what the patient received.

Patient receipt and internal practice notification: Convenience Fee line added

The same breakdown needs to reach every practice-facing email, not just the patient receipt:

Practice emails: “Payment Received” and “Payment Initiated and Processing” variants

Copy changes to know about

  • “Payment Received” (bank-paid): rename the generic “Fee” label to “Processing Fee”; show bank details (e.g. “STRIPE TEST BANK ****6789”) in the Payment Method field.

  • “Payment Received” (card-paid): rename “Amount” to “Service Amount”; add a “Convenience Fee” line before Net Amount.

  • “Payment Initiated and Processing”: add an “Initiated On” timestamp so practices can see exactly when a bank payment entered processing.

Talk track

Q: The patient lost their receipt. Where can they find it again?

A: Every receipt is also viewable from the Payment Details page. Pull up the transaction and click Receipt to resend or download it.

Q: Why does the email say “Processing Fee” instead of “Convenience Fee”?

A: Processing Fee refers to Adit’s own cost of running the transaction (shown on bank payments, which never carry a Convenience Fee); Convenience Fee is the separate, patient-facing charge shown only on card payments.

4. Get Started

Why it matters: this is a new practice’s first exposure to Convenience Fees and Bank/ACH. Getting the onboarding copy and defaults right here prevents a wave of “how do I turn this off” tickets in week one.

Walkthrough

  1. During onboarding, a new practice reaches Adit Pay Set Up -> Step 4 (Payments).

  2. Point out the Convenience Fees block and the Bank/ACH block. Both are mirrored from Preferences (Section 5), so nothing here should surprise a practice that already explored settings.

  3. If the practice merges a direct/offline payment into an open request that has a Convenience Fee, walk them through the Merge Payment confirmation before they click through it.

  4. At Step 5, review the state-exclusion tooltip with the practice if their location is in a restricted state.

Getting Started: Step 4 (Payments), including the new Merge Payment edge case

EDGE CASE: MERGING PAYMENTS “This payment request has a Convenience Fee, but the selected direct payment that you have received does not include a Convenience Fee. To continue merging, the Convenience Fee will be removed from the payment request. Do you want to continue?”. Yes/No. This explains why a merged payment’s total can drop after merging. It is expected behavior, not a bug.

Getting Started: Step 5, showing the state-exclusion tooltip

Talk track

Q: We’re based in Massachusetts. Can we still use Bank/ACH even though Convenience Fees are blocked?

A: Yes. The state exclusion only applies to Convenience Fees. Bank/ACH is available everywhere Adit Pay operates, regardless of state.

Q: I merged a payment and the total changed. Is that a bug?

A: No. That’s the Merge Payment behavior. If the direct payment you merged in didn’t include a Convenience Fee, the system removes the fee from the request rather than leaving a mismatched total.

5. Preferences

Why it matters: every Convenience Fee and Bank/ACH rule in this manual is configured from one screen. If you can’t confidently navigate this page field by field, you can’t troubleshoot anything downstream of it.

Walkthrough

  1. Open Adit Pay -> Preferences -> Payment Request.

  2. Locate “Pass Through Adit Fees to Patient? (Convenience Fees)” and note the main toggle plus the “for One-Time Payments” sub-toggle.

  3. Read the fee note aloud when coaching a new agent: 2.25% + $0.20 for card-present, 2.9% + $0.30 for card-not-present.

  4. Scroll to “Payment and Subscription Plans” and check the “Allow Bank/ACH Payments” and “Allow manual verifications” toggles.

  5. Scroll to “Allow Partial Payments” near the bottom. It should be greyed out automatically whenever Convenience Fees is on.

Preferences: full settings screen with Convenience Fee and Bank/ACH blocks

The two validation modals every agent should recognize

  • Trying to turn ON Partial Payments while Convenience Fees is already on: “Apologies, you are unable to turn on partial payments while you have convenience fees enabled. Would you like to proceed with turning off convenience fees and disabling partial payments?” (No/Yes)

  • Trying to turn OFF Convenience Fees after it’s been in use: an “Are you sure?” confirmation, since disabling it affects every open request currently carrying the fee.

See Appendix A for the complete field-by-field reference of this settings page.

Talk track

Q: Why can’t I turn on Partial Payments?

A: Partial Payments and Convenience Fees are mutually exclusive. Turning one on requires turning the other off, since a partial payment can’t cleanly carry a proportional fee. The system will offer to disable Convenience Fees for you if you confirm.

Q: If I turn off Convenience Fees, what happens to requests that already have the fee applied?

A: You’ll see a confirmation warning before this takes effect. Worth reading carefully, since it affects every currently-open request with the fee attached, not just new ones going forward.

6. Payment Request

Why it matters: agents create and edit payment requests constantly. Getting the Convenience Fee toggle behavior right here avoids both accidentally charging a fee a practice didn’t want, and accidentally forgetting one they did.

Walkthrough

  1. From Payments -> Unpaid, click the pencil (edit) icon on any open request.

  2. The “Include Convenience Fee” checkbox should default to the location’s Preferences setting: checked if Preferences has it on, hidden entirely if Preferences has it off.

  3. Change the Amount field and watch the Convenience Fee and Final Amount recalculate live beneath the checkbox.

  4. If the patient already has another open request, the system treats the existing amount as the base “service amount” and applies the fee to the full new combined total. It isn’t recalculated per line.

Editing an open Payment Request: Include Convenience Fee toggle

Talk track

Q: I don’t see the Convenience Fee option when editing this request. Is that broken?

A: Check Preferences first. If Convenience Fees is toggled off for this location, the section is hidden by design, not missing due to a bug.

Q: The patient already owed money before this new request. Will they get charged the fee twice?

A: No. The system treats their existing open balance as the base amount and applies one fee to the combined total, not one fee per request.

7. Charge Payment on File > Create Payment Flow

Why it matters: this is the highest-frequency in-person collection flow. Agents need to move through it without hesitating over which button does what. The old “Charge Card” label is gone.

Walkthrough

  1. From a patient’s chart, choose Select Payment Method -> “Charge Payment on File” (renamed from “Charge Card”; description now reads “Charge card or bank on file”).

  2. If no method is on file, you’ll be blocked with “You need at least one payment method on file to proceed”. Click Add to open the Add Card modal.

  3. Fill in Name on Card, Cardholder Email, Phone, Credit Card Number, Exp Date, CVV, and Billing Address, then choose whether to set it as the default method.

  4. Once a card is on file, look for the “Convenience Fee Applied” badge next to it if the fee is active for this location.

  5. Move to Confirm Charge and check that Service Amount, Convenience Fee, and Total Amount all match what you quoted the patient verbally.

  6. Click Charge, and wait for both the green “Payment Successful!” screen and the toast “Payment was made successfully!” before ending the interaction.

Create Payment flow: select method, add/charge card, confirm charge

Toasts to recognize

  • Success: “The payment method was added successfully!” / “The payment method was deleted successfully!” / “The payment method was updated successfully!” / “Payment was made successfully!”

  • Failure: “There was an issue with saving this payment method. Please try again!”. If a patient sees this twice in a row, escalate rather than retry a third time.

Talk track

Q: Where did “Charge Card” go? I can’t find it in the menu.

A: It’s been renamed to “Charge Payment on File”. Same place in the menu, now covers both card and bank methods, not just card.

Q: Do I need to tell the patient about the Convenience Fee before charging?

A: Yes. Always confirm the Total Amount (which includes the fee) verbally before clicking Charge, since the patient authorized the service amount, not necessarily the fee.

8. Manual Card Entry

Why it matters: this is the fallback when a terminal isn’t available or a card can’t be saved to file. Agents need to know exactly when to check the “save on file” box.

Walkthrough

  1. Select Payment Method -> Manual Card Entry.

  2. Enter the payment amount context. It should already reflect the Convenience Fee if one applies (e.g. $10.00 service becomes $10.61 total).

  3. Complete the card and billing fields.

  4. Check “Save Payment Method on Patient’s File” only if the patient has explicitly agreed to keep the card on file for future charges. This is opt-in, not default.

  5. Click Process. The “Payment Successful!” screen should show Service Amount, Convenience Fee, and Total Amount separately.

Manual Card Entry: worked example: $10.00 service + fee = $10.61 total

Talk track

Q: Is the card automatically saved after a manual entry charge?

A: No. Only if the “Save Payment Method on Patient’s File” checkbox was checked before processing. Always confirm with the patient before checking it.

9. Charge Payment on File > Collect Payment Flow

Why it matters: this is the single best flow to point to when explaining the “no fee on ACH” rule, since the card and bank outcomes are built from the exact same screen and only one carries a fee line.

Walkthrough

  1. From an existing open balance, choose Collect Payment.

  2. If Convenience Fees applies, the “Include Convenience Fee” checkbox should show both the card-present and card-not-present fee amounts side by side (e.g. “$29.30 (CNP $30.18)”). This dual display is intentional, not a duplicate bug.

  3. Select a payment method. For Card, move to Confirm Charge and check that the receipt shows Service Amount / Convenience Fee / Total Amount.

  4. For Bank, the outcome screen should instead read “Bank Payment Processing” with Service Amount / Total Amount only. No Convenience Fee line at all.

Collect Payment flow: card outcome carries a Convenience Fee line; bank outcome doesn’t

Collect Payment: clean entry point, from the full Figma export

Talk track

Q: The fee amount shown has two numbers next to it. Is that a glitch?

A: No. That’s showing the card-present amount and the card-not-present amount together (e.g. “$29.30 (CNP $30.18)”) so the agent can see both before knowing which rate will apply.

Q: Why didn’t the bank payment confirmation show a fee?

A: By design. Convenience Fees never apply to Bank/ACH payments, so the bank confirmation screen omits that line entirely rather than showing $0.00.

10. Bulk Payment Request

Why it matters: one misconfigured bulk send can put an incorrect fee in front of dozens of patients at once. This is the highest-blast-radius flow in the whole product.

Walkthrough

  1. From Payments, select multiple patients and choose Bulk Payment Request.

  2. Choose Send Via (Text / Email / Voice) and Message Priority, then edit the text and email templates using the merge-field chips provided (never hand-type a patient’s name).

  3. Click Next to reach “Confirm Request Amount.”

  4. If Convenience Fees is off for this send, the table should show only EHR Balance / Existing Adit Pay Balance / New Adit Pay Balance.

  5. If Convenience Fees is on, two extra columns should appear: Conv Fee and Total Adit Pay Amt Due. A patient with no new balance due should show “-” in both, not a $0.00 row.

  6. Click Send only after spot-checking at least one patient’s calculated fee against the formulas in Section 1.

Bulk Payment Request: Without Con Fee / With Con Fee (toggled off) / With Con Fee (on by default)

Talk track

Q: Can I send a bulk request to some patients with the fee and others without?

A: No. The Convenience Fee toggle applies to the entire bulk send. If some patients need different treatment, split them into separate sends.

Q: One patient in my list shows a dash instead of a dollar amount for their fee. Is that an error?

A: No. A dash means that patient has no new balance due, so there’s nothing to calculate a fee against. It’s intentional, not a missing value.

11. One-Time Payment Page (Text to Pay)

Why it matters: this is the only page most patients ever see. Every method offered here needs to be treated consistently, or Adit risks a real compliance problem, not just a support ticket (see QA-3).

Walkthrough

  1. Send a patient a Text-to-Pay link and open it as they would.

  2. The header should show Balance Due, Convenience Fee, and Payment Amount together.

  3. Check that every listed method (Apple Pay, Google Pay, CareCredit, Credit Card) is labeled consistently for whether a Convenience Fee applies (see the flag below before assuming any single method is exempt).

  4. Select Credit Card. The inline form (Cardholder Name, Email, Card Number, Exp/CVV, Billing Address, Save Card on File) should expand on the same page without a redirect.

  5. If the patient already has a card on file, “Payment methods you have on file with us” should list it with a way to set a new default or pay with a new card.

Payment methods on the public page: Apple Pay, Google Pay, CareCredit, Credit Card

FLAG FOR REVIEW This screen labels Apple Pay “Without Convenience Fee” while Google Pay on the same screen is labeled “Convenience Fee applied.” Card network rules require the fee to apply uniformly across every method in a channel. Confirm with design whether this is only illustrating two label states for review, or literal differing default behavior per method: treat as a compliance risk until confirmed.

One-Time Payments Page: with/without a card on file, “Use Another Card” path

Additional One-Time Payment Page variant, from the full Figma export

Talk track

Watch for: the public payment page showing different Convenience Fee labels for different payment methods (e.g. Apple Pay vs. Google Pay).

This is an open design question (see QA-3), not confirmed live behavior. If a patient asks, tell them the fee applies the same way regardless of payment method, and escalate any live discrepancy immediately.

Q: Can the patient pay less than the full balance from this page?

A: Not with Convenience Fees enabled. Partial payments are automatically disabled whenever the fee is on (see Section 5).

12. Payment Plans

Why it matters: this is the mirror image of Section 11. Convenience Fee is blocked here, Bank/ACH is welcomed. Mixing up these two rules in a patient conversation is the single most common agent error to coach against.

Walkthrough

  1. From Payment Plans, open or create a plan and reach Step 3: Payment Details.

  2. Choose “Manually Add Payment Method” or “Request Payment Method from Patient.”

  3. If adding manually, choose Card or Bank in the Add Payment Method modal and complete the relevant fields.

  4. A plan can carry both a saved card and a saved bank account at the same time. The “one bank account” limit is about bank accounts specifically, not a total cap.

  5. To remove a saved method, the Confirm Delete modal (“This action cannot be undone”) should appear before it’s removed.

Payment Plans: practice-side list view, from the full Figma export

Setting up a Payment Plan: manual add vs. request from patient

Managing saved payment methods on a plan: copy updates and Confirm Delete

Requesting a payment method from a patient: a plan can hold a saved card AND a saved bank account at once

Talk track

Q: Can we add a Convenience Fee to this payment plan like we do for one-time payments?

A: No. Convenience Fees are never available on payment plans or subscriptions, by card network rule. Bank/ACH is the low-cost alternative offered here instead.

Q: The patient already has a card on file. Can they also add a bank account?

A: Yes. A plan can hold one saved bank account and any number of saved cards simultaneously.

IMPORTANT CONTEXT: TWO DIFFERENT BANK-PAYMENT SYSTEMS “Bank/ACH” is not one system. The US uses “Instant Bank Payments” via Stripe Link: the patient authenticates with their bank and the payment confirms in seconds, settling in about 2 days, with Stripe guaranteeing the payment against bank-initiated failures like insufficient funds. Canada uses a separate, slower rail called ACSS: about 5 business days to settle, no instant option, and a payment CAN be returned after it already showed as “succeeded.” Sections 13 and 14 below map to these two systems respectively, though the exact mapping of the manual-verification screens to one system or the other is flagged as needing confirmation (see QA-1 and QA-8).

13. Payment Plans > Bank Instant Verification Flow

Why it matters: this is the US rail (“Instant Bank Payments” via Stripe Link) that patients will use most often to pay a plan by bank, since it confirms in seconds rather than days. Agents should be able to narrate every screen a patient might be stuck on over the phone, and know its real-world limits.

Walkthrough

  1. On the patient’s own plan page, they should see Plan Name, Frequency, Recurring Charges, and “Payment Due Today,” with Pay With Credit Card and Pay With Bank/ACH Payment options.

  2. If they choose Add Bank/ACH Payment, walk them through: “Log in to Bank (OAuth)” loading screen -> their bank’s own login window -> “Retrieving accounts…” loading screen.

  3. Once accounts load, the patient selects the specific account (e.g. “Stripebank ****6789”) and confirms.

  4. On success, they should see “Your Payment Plan is now Active!” with the option to review the plan or add a secondary card.

  5. On the practice side, the Payment Plan Detail Page should show the matching Processing -> Successful states as the bank payment clears.

Patient plan page and Bank Instant Verification: OAuth login through account confirmation

Payment Plan Detail Page: practice-side Processing/Successful bank states, from the full Figma export

“Finish Setting Up Your Payment Plan!” reminder: shown when bank verification was started but never completed

What makes this rail different from a card

  • Settlement takes about 2 days, but the payment shows as confirmed immediately. Stripe guarantees the payment against bank-initiated failures (insufficient funds, etc.), so unlike traditional ACH, a successful Instant Bank Payment generally will not bounce back later for those reasons.

  • A patient-initiated dispute is still possible and is handled like a card dispute (evidence can be submitted), but funds are pulled from the practice while it’s under review.

  • There is a per-transaction cap on this rail (commonly cited around $7,500, though Stripe sets it dynamically per account and it isn’t publicly documented). Above the cap, or if the practice/transaction isn’t eligible, the recommended fallback is card, not a slower ACH path.

  • The patient must authenticate through Stripe’s Link screen on their own device. This likely means in-office/front-desk bank payment isn’t a tap-through-the-terminal experience the way a card is; the practical path is texting or emailing the patient a link to complete on their phone (see QA-15).

Talk track

Q: The patient says they’re stuck on a loading screen after logging into their bank. What’s happening?

A: That’s the “Retrieving accounts…” step, which pulls the linked accounts from their bank via Stripe. If it hangs for more than a minute, have them close and restart the Add Bank flow rather than wait indefinitely.

Q: The patient started adding a bank account but never finished. Will anything remind them?

A: Yes. They’ll receive a “Finish Setting Up Your Payment Plan!” email if verification was started but not completed.

Q: Can a patient pay a large treatment balance by bank?

A: Only up to the per-transaction cap on this rail. For anything above it, the recommended path is card, not a slower bank transfer, so set that expectation with the patient before they try to link a bank account for a very large balance.

Q: Can we run this at the front desk like a card payment?

A: Likely not directly. The patient authenticates through their bank’s own login on their own device, so the practical in-office path is sending them a link to complete on their phone rather than having them do it on the practice’s terminal.

14. Payment Plan > Bank Manual Verification Flow

NO SCREENSHOT SHARED YET FOR THIS SECTION No screenshot of the manual (micro-deposit) verification screens themselves has been found in either the shared screenshots or the Figma export: neither includes an “Add Bank” or “Verify Bank Account” frame for this specific path. The walkthrough below is built from the Figma design notes and the earlier API review. The two images below are the closest adjacent frames available: the failure state and setup reminder this flow can lead to: not the entry/verification screens themselves.
OPEN QUESTION: IS THIS FLOW US OR CANADA? The source Q&A document notes that the US rail (Instant Bank Payments) is meant to be the only US path going forward, with the slower fallback “off the table unless Product explicitly reopens it.” That raises a real possibility that this micro-deposit flow actually represents Canada’s ACSS verification path rather than a general US fallback; the same document says this needs to be confirmed with Stripe directly. Train agents on the mechanics below, but don’t assert to a practice which country/rail this applies to until it’s confirmed.

Walkthrough (from design notes: confirm against the live product before training verbatim)

  1. Patient chooses Bank/ACH but their bank isn’t available for instant login, or they decline to log in. This routes them to manual entry.

  2. Patient enters Routing Number, Account Number, and Confirm Account Number.

  3. Stripe sends two small deposits (or a descriptor code) to the account. This typically takes 1-2 business days.

  4. Patient returns to the plan page and enters the two deposit amounts (or descriptor code) to confirm ownership.

  5. Once verified, the account behaves identically to an instantly-verified one for future payments.

  • The “Allow manual verifications” toggle in Preferences controls whether this path is offered at all for a given location.

If this is Canada (ACSS): what’s different from the US rail

  • Settlement takes about 5 business days rather than about 2.

  • Unlike the US rail, a Canada payment is NOT guaranteed. It can fail for insufficient funds, an invalid account number, or the customer disabling debits, and it can be returned even after it already showed as “succeeded” (this surfaces as a dispute-like event and reverses the payment).

  • Dispute windows are long: 90 days for personal accounts, 10 business days for business accounts, and disputes are described as “no questions asked,” meaning the practice cannot contest them the way a US bank dispute can be evidenced.

  • A cross-currency debit (for example, a Canadian account charged in USD) is called out as a common source of a payment failing about 5 days after it looked successful.

  • This rail does not support manual capture (auth-then-capture), and an authorization/mandate on one connected account cannot be reused if a patient moves to a different practice location on a different connected account.

Payment Error with your Payment Plan: the failure state this flow can lead to

Payment Failed: patient-facing email tied to a failed scheduled payment

Talk track

Q: The patient entered their micro-deposit amounts and it says they don’t match. What now?

A: Confirm they’re reading amounts in cents correctly (e.g. “32” and “45,” not “$0.32” and “$0.45” typed as dollars). If it still fails, the most common root cause is a typo in the original routing/account number. Have them re-add the bank account rather than keep retrying the same deposit amounts.

Q: A Canadian patient’s payment showed as successful last week and now it’s reversed. Is that a bug?

A: Not necessarily. Unlike the US rail, ACSS payments in Canada aren’t guaranteed and can be returned days after they first cleared. Check whether it’s a bank-side return or a customer dispute before treating it as an error.

15. Patient Card

NO SCREENSHOT SHARED YET FOR THIS SECTION No screenshot literally titled “Patient Card” has been found in either the shared screenshots or the Figma export. It appears embedded within the Charge Payment on File flow (Section 7) as the “one card on file” panel. The two images below are the closest matching frames available in the export.

What to know

  • A maximum of 10 cards are allowed on file per patient. Once reached, the “add” and “request” options grey out, with a tooltip explaining the limit. This applies everywhere a card can be added, not just one screen.

  • The card list initially shows 3 cards on file; beyond that, a “show more cards on file” option expands the rest.

  • Only ONE bank account can be saved at a time. This is the one asymmetry between cards and bank accounts worth remembering.

  • In dental specifically, the person paying is often not the patient being treated (a parent, guardian, or other guarantor). Whose bank account or card counts as “on file,” and how it maps to the patient being treated, is called out in the source product Q&A as still needing a decision (see QA-16).

Save Card on File: closest matching frame from the full Figma export

“Card Requested” notification

Talk track

Q: The practice can’t add another card for this patient. Why?

A: They’ve likely hit the 10-card limit. Have them remove an unused saved card first, or confirm with the patient which one to delete.

16. Treatment Plans

Why it matters: the Treatment Plan builder is where a practice first proposes a payment structure to a patient. A missing Convenience Fee option here means the practice has to explain the fee separately later, which is a worse patient experience than seeing it up front.

Walkthrough

  1. Open Treatment Plans -> Tx Plan Builder and select or create a plan.

  2. Build out the treatment option(s), fee structure, and discount as needed.

  3. In Payment Options, choose One-Time Payment or Payment in Installments (with configurable frequency and number of payments).

  4. In Payment Method, confirm Credit Card, Bank/ACH, Check, and Cash are all available. And that a Convenience Fee option is present alongside them once added.

  5. Complete consent and signature steps as required before sending or saving.

Treatment Plan Builder: Payment Method section needs a “Convenience Fee” addition

Talk track

Q: Can a treatment plan use the same Convenience Fee rules as a one-time payment?

A: Once added, yes. But confirm which payment option the patient chose first (one-time vs. installments), since installments follow the Payment Plan rule (no Convenience Fee, Bank/ACH allowed) rather than the one-time rule.

Part 2: QA Test Plan & Findings

This part has two halves: a structured set of test cases an agent or QA tester can run directly, and a findings list. Each with the evidence behind it and a recommended action, not just an observation.

2.2 Findings

Each finding includes what evidence it’s based on and a recommended next step. Treat these as tickets to triage, not just observations.

Adit-Pay-ACH-and-CF-Training-QA-Manual (continued, part 1)

QA-1 “Returned after success” risk is real for Canada, likely already handled for the US [NEEDS CONFIRMATION] Finding: Earlier framing treated this as a single open gap across all bank payments. Reading the source Q&A doc more closely splits it in two: the US rail (Instant Bank Payments) is guaranteed by Stripe against bank-initiated failures, so a successful payment generally should not bounce back for that reason (a customer-initiated dispute is still possible, handled like a card dispute). Canada (ACSS) has no such guarantee and explicitly CAN return after already showing “succeeded,” including from cross-currency debits. Evidence: Payment Plan Detail Page states (Section 13), Payment Error / Payment Failed frames (Section 14), and the “Adit Pay: Bank Payments: Questions for Product & Design” document, Sections 3 and 7. Recommended action: For the US, treat this as lower risk given Stripe’s guarantee, but confirm the dispute-driven reversal path is designed. For Canada, confirm a distinct “Processing vs. Paid” status and a reopen/notify-staff path exist for a late return, since that document flags it as still an open decision (its own Q15).
QA-2 Payments list mock data shows a fee on Bank-method rows [NEEDS CONFIRMATION] Finding: Example data in the Payments list includes rows where Method = “Bank” but the Conv. Fee column still shows a non-zero value. Evidence: Section 1 screenshot. Rows for Ginger Vitis and Pearl White show Method: Bank with non-zero Conv. Fee values, contradicting the documented rule that fees never apply to Bank/ACH. Recommended action: Confirm this is placeholder/lorem data only. If any test fixtures were derived from this mock, regenerate them with $0/blank fees on Bank rows before using them for QA.
QA-3 Public payment page shows different fee treatment per method [NEEDS CONFIRMATION] Finding: Apple Pay is labeled “Without Convenience Fee” while Google Pay on the same screen is labeled “Convenience Fee applied.” Evidence: Section 11 screenshot, “Adit Payments Page”. Both labels visible side by side on the same mockup. Recommended action: Confirm with design whether this is illustrating two label states for sign-off purposes only. If it reflects real default behavior, escalate as a compliance risk before launch. Card network rules require uniform treatment across methods in a channel.
QA-4 Disable-Convenience-Fee confirmation copy looks unfinished [LOW] Finding: The “Are you sure?” modal shown when disabling Convenience Fees in Preferences reads as draft/placeholder text rather than final copy. Evidence: Section 5 screenshot, right-side annotation callouts on the Preferences page. Recommended action: Route to whoever owns UX copy for a final pass before this ships, given it’s a compliance-adjacent confirmation.
QA-5 Confirm: a plan can hold both a card AND a bank account [INFO] Finding: A plan’s “Request Payment Method from Patient” view shows both a card and a bank account saved simultaneously. Evidence: Section 12 screenshot. Two saved methods (•9876 card, •1234 bank) shown together on the same plan. Recommended action: State this explicitly in the public help article and internal training: one bank account maximum, any number of cards, both types can coexist on a single plan.
QA-6 Merge Payment fee-removal needs a support-facing explanation [LOW] Finding: The Merge Payment confirmation (Section 4) silently removes a Convenience Fee from a request when the merged-in direct payment doesn’t include one. Evidence: Section 4 screenshot, “Merge Payment” modal copy. Recommended action: Add a line about this behavior to the public Convenience Fee help article and to this manual’s talk track, so it isn’t reported as a billing discrepancy.
QA-7 “3-4 business day” bank-processing copy may be stale [NEEDS CONFIRMATION] Finding: The patient-facing line “Bank payments typically take 3-4 business days to process!” is a specific, quotable SLA that was written before the product’s shift toward “Instant Bank Payments” for the US. Evidence: Design annotation from the original Figma review, compared against the “Adit Pay: Bank Payments: Questions for Product & Design” document, which states the US rail settles in about 2 days with instant confirmation, and Canada (ACSS) settles in about 5 business days. Recommended action: Check whether this copy is still shown anywhere in the live product. If so, it likely needs to be split by country (fast confirmation for US, ~5 business days for Canada) rather than shown as one blanket figure.
QA-8 Two sections still lack a matching screenshot [FOLLOW-UP] Finding: Patient Card (Section 15) and Payment Plan > Bank Manual Verification Flow (Section 14) have no screenshot literally matching their name in either the shared screenshots or the full Figma export. Evidence: Exhaustive filename search of both the 19 shared screenshots and the ~500-file Figma export turned up no “Add Bank” / “Verify Bank Account” (manual) or standalone “Patient Card” frame. Recommended action: Export and share these two specifically from Figma if they exist elsewhere in the file; otherwise confirm with design whether they were ever built as distinct frames.
QA-9 KPI tiles for “Convenience Fees” and “Processing Fees” show identical values [NEEDS CONFIRMATION] Finding: The Payments list KPI row shows Convenience Fees and Processing Fees both at $300.50 in the same example. Evidence: Section 1 screenshot, top KPI tiles. Recommended action: Confirm these are tracked as independent totals in the live data and this is coincidental test data, not two tiles reading from the same underlying field.
QA-10 Naming inconsistency between “Add Card” and “Add Payment Method” [LOW] Finding: The Create Payment flow’s modal is titled “Add Card,” while the visually near-identical modal in the Collect Payment flow is titled “Add Payment Method.” Evidence: Compare Section 7 (“Add Card”) against Section 9 (“Add Payment Method”) screenshots. Recommended action: Confirm whether this is an intentional naming difference (e.g. one flow supports bank, the other doesn’t) or a copy inconsistency that should be unified.
QA-11 Possible layering artifacts in the One-Time Payment Page mockup [LOW] Finding: Some variants of the public one-time payment page show visually duplicated headers and fields (e.g. practice name or balance appearing twice stacked). Evidence: Section 11 screenshot, “One-Time Payments Page” variants. Duplicated “ABC Family Dentistry” header and duplicated PAY button visible in at least one crop. Recommended action: Confirm this is a Figma layering artifact from overlapping mockup states, not a real rendering duplication bug, before treating it as representative of production behavior.
QA-12 Bulk Payment Request patient count differs across the three fee-state examples [INFO] Finding: The “Without Fee” and “Toggled Off” mockups show 3 example patients; the “Toggled On” mockup shows 5, adding two more to demonstrate a zero-fee and a partial-fee case. Evidence: Section 10 screenshot, three “Confirm Request Amount” variants. Recommended action: Likely intentional (extra rows added to showcase edge cases) rather than a data inconsistency. Confirm with whoever built the mockup, and reuse those extra rows as the basis for TC-14.
QA-13 Product’s own checklist: four bank-payment items not yet confirmed in Figma [FOLLOW-UP] Finding: The source Q&A document includes a “feature parity” checklist, written by the product team itself, listing bank-related items not yet confirmed present in the new designs: (1) a bank-payment transaction detail page showing bank name, last 4, and status; (2) refund behavior for bank payments; (3) the warning shown when removing a card or bank account tied to a payment plan; (4) Download Statement on the patient page. Evidence: “Adit Pay: Bank Payments: Questions for Product & Design,” Section 11. Recommended action: Treat these four as open items rather than assuming the reviewed screenshots cover them. Confirm each directly with design, since this is a more authoritative source than screenshot-coverage gaps alone.
QA-14 Per-transaction cap and over-cap fallback not visible in any reviewed screen [NEEDS CONFIRMATION] Finding: The US rail (Instant Bank Payments) has a per-transaction cap (commonly cited around $7,500), above which the recommended behavior is falling back to card. No reviewed screenshot shows this cap, an over-cap message, or the fallback prompt. Evidence: “Adit Pay: Bank Payments: Questions for Product & Design,” cover briefing and Question 2. Recommended action: Confirm the cap value and the over-cap patient-facing experience (Question 16 in that document) are designed before this ships, since dental treatment balances can plausibly exceed it.
QA-15 In-office bank payment scope is unclear [NEEDS CONFIRMATION] Finding: Instant Bank Payments requires the patient to authenticate through Stripe’s Link screen on their own device. No reviewed screenshot shows how (or whether) a front-desk agent initiates a bank payment in person, as opposed to sending the patient a link to complete on their phone. Evidence: “Adit Pay: Bank Payments: Questions for Product & Design,” Question 10, explicitly flagged as an open UX decision. Recommended action: Confirm whether in-office bank payment is in scope at all for the initial release, and if so, how an agent triggers the text/email-to-phone flow from the front desk.
QA-16 Guarantor billing and bank auto-charge order are still open product questions [FOLLOW-UP] Finding: Two related items from the source document aren’t reflected anywhere in the reviewed designs or this manual’s original content: who a saved bank account belongs to when the payer isn’t the patient (a parent or guardian, common in dental), and where bank sits in the automatic charge order relative to a patient’s saved cards (today: selected card, then default card, then backup cards). Evidence: “Adit Pay: Bank Payments: Questions for Product & Design,” Questions 21 and 24. Recommended action: Both are explicitly called out as undecided in the source document. Flag to product rather than assuming an answer when training agents on guarantor accounts or fallback billing.

Adit-Pay-ACH-and-CF-Training-QA-Manual (continued, part 2)

Appendix B: Fee Formula Reference

The exact math behind every Convenience Fee shown in this manual.

Scenario Formula Worked Example
Card-not-present (2.9% + $0.30) Final Charge = (Desired Amount + $0.30) / (1 - 0.029) $100.00 -> $103.30 charged; processor takes $3.30; practice nets $100.00
Card-present (2.25% + $0.20) Final Charge = (Desired Amount + $0.20) / (1 - 0.0225) $100.00 -> $102.51 charged
ACH transaction cost (not patient-facing) 0.5% + $1.75 per transaction Charged to the practice only when a payment processes. Never at account setup, never to the patient

ACH transaction cost, worked examples

From the Adit Pay ACH Cost calculator: the fee is a straight 0.5% of the transaction plus a flat $1.75, with no gross-up (unlike the card Convenience Fee formulas above, this cost is not passed through to the patient).

Transaction Size Adit Charges the Practice
$100 $2.25
$200 $2.75
$250 $3.00
$272 $3.11
$500 $4.25
$1,000 $6.75

Sources: annotated design-review screenshots shared directly in chat, the Figma “Adit Pay. ACH” file export, the Adit Pay ACH Cost calculator, the “Adit Pay: Bank Payments: Questions for Product & Design” document, and Asana task documentation. Compiled for internal training and QA use.

Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) - Adit Pay Team (Adit Pay)

Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) - Adit Pay Team

Department: Adit Pay

  • Handling Support Tickets - We take inbound calls from clients or call them back if required in order to address/resolve their queries.

  • Demos/Trainings - I handle Adit Pay/Financing Demo and Trainings whenever required and ensure that the process is smooth and hasslefree for the clients.

  • Terminal Registration - We register the terminal once it is delivered to the client and also provide them a short walkthrough on how to process in office payments in addition to training.

  • Assisting Tech OB/Tech CSM - Sometimes we are requested to assist the Tech OBs or Tech CSMs if the client is on call with them and has Adit Pay queries or if they are facing any issues in regards to Adit Pay.

  • Creating Asana Task - I create Asana tasks whenever required and assign it to the respective team for quick and effective resolution of client issues. Some examples of creating tasks are payment posting issues, Client bugs and Terminal/base Station Order.

  • Terminal Issues/Troubleshooting - We also receive calls quite frequently about terminal connectivity issues where the clients face issues to process in office payments.
    We assist them in troubleshooting and once the issue is identified we resolve that and ensure that the client is updated about it.

  • Google Chat - Respond to messages from other groups/individuals and ensure that they are tagged to the concerned person or team.

  • Assigning tickets to the Adit Pay team including me and sharing EOD report on Adit Pay/Agent group.

Adit Call Intelligence Upgrade Sales Playbook (Call Intelligence)

Adit Call Intelligence Upgrade Sales Playbook

Introduction to Call Intelligence

Adit’s Call Intelligence is an AI-powered upgrade to our existing Call Tracking module, designed specifically for dental, optometry, and multi-location practices (including DSOs) to transform how they handle inbound and outbound calls. Built on advanced AI technology, it goes beyond basic call logging by providing automated summaries, transcripts, sentiment analysis, performance scorecards, task creation, and actionable insights. This helps practices capture missed revenue, improve staff performance, enhance patient experiences, and make data-driven decisions without manually listening to every call.

Key benefits include:

  • Revenue Recovery: Identifies unbooked scheduling opportunities, missed calls, and high-value leads (Invisalign or implants) for follow-up.
  • Operational Efficiency: Automates tasks, notifications for upset patients or lost opportunities, and integrates summaries directly into patient profiles in the EHR.
  • Performance Insights: Scores staff on calls, tracks conversions, and provides dashboards for sentiment, call types, and marketing ROI.
  • Seamless Integration: Upgrades the Call Tracking UI with AI features; available per location, with phase 2 enhancements (automatic lead-to-patient conversion) rolling out soon.

Priced as an upgrade, it’s ideal for existing Adit customers already using Call Tracking or phone services. Phase 1 focuses on core AI analysis and reporting; phase 2 adds advanced automation like multi-location dashboards and lead conversion.

This playbook equips Upgrade SDRs and AEs with a step-by-step guide to pitch and sell Call Intelligence, drawing from internal training insights and proven switch factors reasons practices upgrade or switch providers.

The Playbook: How to Pitch and Sell Call Intelligence

Start with preparation, move to discovery and pitching, handle objections, and close. Focus on value over features tie everything to pain points like lost revenue, staff inefficiencies, and lack of visibility. Use the 11 switch factors (Linked Below) as your “winning points” to build urgency. Sell to Office Managers, Doctors, or DSO leaders; avoid front desk staff initially, as they may resist performance tracking.

1. Pre Call Preparation: Know Your Audience and Product

Target Buyers:

  • Office Managers (OMs): Pain points include missed calls, poor follow-ups, upset patients, and inconsistent staff performance. They want tools to streamline operations and prove ROI.
  • Doctors/Owners: Focus on revenue loss, high-value opportunities (e.g., implants, crowns), marketing effectiveness, and compliance (e.g., knowing every interaction).
  • DSOs/Multi-Locations: Emphasize location comparisons, scalable insights, and centralized dashboards (mention phase 2 for multi-location rollouts).

Key Switch Factors to Memorize (Prioritize greens: 1-4, 7-10 for most pitches; yellows: 5-6, 11 for deeper convos):

Call Intelliegence - Switch Factors

Use these as hooks, frame them as questions to uncover pain.

Example: Start with #1 (Missed Revenue): “How many scheduling calls go unbooked each month, and how do you track follow-ups?”

Demo Setup: Use the demo app (Update: blue-tabbed for easy navigation). Show Figma mocks only if necessary for unreleased features. Highlight: Call detail page (summary, transcript, scorecard, tasks), leads dashboard, insights (missed call recovery, scheduling breakdowns), notifications.

Sales Tools:

  • Website page for visuals.(Pending)
  • Switch factors doc for reference. Call Intelliegence - Switch Factors
  • Adit App flags for eligibility (must have Call Tracking active).
  • No free trial blanket case-by-case for upgrades; emphasize immediate value from 30-day retroactive analysis.

2. Discovery: Uncover Pain with Targeted Questions

Discovery is 60% of the sale use open-ended questions based on switch factors to build pain and position Call Intelligence as the fix. Aim for 10-15 minutes; listen more than talk.

Opening Rapport: “I noticed you’re using Adit Call Tracking great foundation. Today, let’s talk about upgrading to AI-powered insights to capture more revenue and streamline your front desk.”

Core Discovery Questions (Group by theme; ask 4-6 per call, probing deeper):

Revenue & Opportunities (#1, #2, #4, #8):

“How many scheduling calls don’t result in bookings each month? How do you follow up?”

“What happens with missed calls? Do you track which ones get called back and converted?”

“How do you spot high-value opportunities like Invisalign or crowns that slip away, and why weren’t they booked?”

“After a call, how do you ensure action items (insurance verifications) don’t fall through?”

Patient Experience & Notifications (#3, #5, #6):

“How do you know if a patient was unhappy during a call before it escalates to a bad review?”

“Is your front desk delivering consistent experiences across new/existing patients or call types (billing vs. scheduling)?”

“How do you keep patient notes updated after every interaction without manual work?”

Staff Performance & Training (#7):

“How often do you review staff calls for improvements? If you retrain, how do you measure progress?”

Data & ROI (#9, #10, #11):

“Which marketing channels convert best? If one fails, is it lead gen or front desk conversion and why?”

“How do you make decisions on staffing, services, or insurances based on call data?”

“For your locations, how do you compare front desk performance side-by-side?”

Probing Tips: Follow up with “Tell me more” or “What impact does that have on revenue?” Quantify pain: “If you miss 50 calls/month, that’s potentially $10,000 in lost appointments.”

Transition to Pitch: “Based on what you’ve shared about (pain point), Call Intelligence directly addresses that by (tease value). Let me show you how.”

3. Pitching: Build Value with Stories and Demos

Keep pitches 15-20 minutes; use storytelling from training (“Practices miss 50+ calls a month during business hours, imagine recovering that revenue”). Focus on 3-5 switch factors per pitch, tailored to discovery. Structure: Problem → Solution → Benefit → Proof.

Pitch Framework:

Hook with Pain: Start with a stat: “Most practices lose 60% of potential revenue from unbooked calls and inconsistent follow-ups.”

Overview Value Prop: “Call Intelligence uses AI to analyze every call in real-time, providing summaries, sentiments, tasks, and insights so you never miss revenue, upset patients, or training opportunities.”

Demo Walkthrough (Use app/Figma):

Call Detail Page: “Here’s a call, AI summarizes it, detects sentiment (green=happy, red=unhappy), scores staff ( rapport, empathy), and creates tasks like ‘Follow up on billing issue.’

Leads Dashboard: “Unbooked calls become leads here, sorted by revenue potential. Phase 2 auto-converts to patients in your EHR.”

Insights & Reporting: “See new patient bookings, missed call recovery (click to view unreturned calls), conversion rates (inbound vs. outbound), and marketing sources.”

Notifications: “Get instant emails for upset patients or lost high-value ops with summary and transcript snippets.”

Integration: “Summaries push to patient notes in EHR for quick reference, no manual updates.” (Phase 2)

Tailored Stories:

Adit Call Intelligence Upgrade Sales Playbook (continued, part 1)

  • For OMs: “Imagine Friday at 5 PM, check missed calls dashboard, see unreturned ones, assign tasks instantly.”

  • For Doctors: “A patient calls for a $3K implant but doesn’t book, AI flags it, shows reason (insurance), and creates a follow-up task.”

  • For DSOs: “Compare locations: Location A converts 70% of scheduling calls, Location B only 50%, drill down to staff scores and sentiments.”
    Quantify ROI: “Practices recover 10-20% more appointments; reduce bad reviews by catching unhappy calls early; improve staff conversion by 15% via scoring.”

Pitch Script Example (Short Version for SDRs): “Dr. [Name], from our conversation today, missed follow-ups are costing you potential revenue. With Call Intelligence, AI analyzes calls to spot unbooked opportunities, creates automated tasks, and notifies you of high-value losses. Let me demo: Here’s a scheduling call summary showing “not booked due to availability”, revenue potential $500, task auto-assigned. This ensures nothing slips through want to see your data applied?”

4. Objection Handling: Turn Doubts into Closes

Common objections from training insights respond with empathy, restate value, and ask for commitment.

“Too Expensive/We Don’t Need It”: “Upgrades add cost, but consider the ROI. If you recover just 5 appointments/month at $200 each, it pays for itself. Plus, no manual call reviews saves hours. Shall we run a quick calculation based on your call volume?”

“Our Staff Already Handles This”: “That’s great they’re proactive, but even top teams miss visibility. AI scores every call and tracks conversions without listening, empowering better training. Have you measured outbound scheduling success lately?”

“Not Ready for AI/Privacy Concerns”: “AI is secure and compliant; we use voiceprints for accuracy, not storage. It starts with simple summaries and tasks building to full insights. Many practices start with one location to test.”

“What About Phase 2 Features?”: “Core features like summaries and notifications are live now; phase 2 (auto-lead conversion) launches Soon, enhancing what you get today. We can onboard with phase 1 and upgrade seamlessly.”

“We Have Something Similar”: “RingCentral summaries voicemails, but Call Intelligence analyzes full calls, creates EHR-integrated tasks, and provides staff scoring, addressing switch factors like upset notifications that others miss.”

5. Closing: Secure the Upgrade

Trial Close: After demo: “How does this address your missed revenue challenges?”

Assumptive Close: “Based on this, upgrading one location makes sense, let’s flag it in CRM and get started.”

Urgency: “With phase 2 imminent, now’s ideal to lock in; plus, we’ll analyze your last 30 days’ calls for instant insights.”

Next Steps: Send agreement (same as other upgrades), schedule onboarding. Follow up weekly first 30-60 days to refine based on wins/losses.

Metrics for Success: Track: Discovery-to-Demo Rate (80%), Demo-to-Close (40%), Average Deal Size (per location).

Review this playbook weekly; adapt based on real calls. Share wins in team chats let’s crush upgrades!
